messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing a psychological case vignette
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

Write a realistic clinical case vignette for a patient with PTSD.
The vignette should read as a cohesive, flowing portrait — not a structured report.
Weave together who this person is, what happened to them, how they experience their
symptoms day to day, how they cope, and what toll this takes on their life and relationships.


Do not use section headers, numbered points, or clinical labels for symptoms.
Write 200–300 words in third person.
Cover: presenting complaints, trauma background, cognitive distortions, avoidance, and maintaining factors.
Avoid excessive jargon - write for a clinical case conference audience.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient presenting with PTSD.
Patient demographics:
- Age: 35
- Gender: Male
- Ethnicity: European
- Relationship Status: Single
- Occupation: Special Education Teacher
- Trauma Type: Mugging or robbery
- Pcl5: 58

Thomas is a 35-year-old special education teacher who has always found joy in his work, believing in the potential of each of his students. He recalls the warmth of their laughter and the moments of breakthrough when a child finally grasps a difficult concept. But since that fateful night, his classroom has become a shadow of its former self.

It all began three months ago when Thomas was walking home from a late meeting at school. He recalls the crisp air, the sound of leaves crunching underfoot, and the faint chatter of people in the distance. He feels a sense of comfort in his routine, the familiarity of the path he has walked countless times before. But on this evening, as he turns a corner, he notices two figures lurking in the shadows. A chill runs down his spine as he instinctively senses something is wrong.

Before he can react, the figures approach him. Adrenaline surges through his body as their faces twist into malicious grins. They demand his wallet, their voices low and threatening. In that moment, time seems to stretch; he feels trapped within his own body, as if he is watching the scene unfold from a distance. The fear is palpable; his heart pounds violently against his ribcage. When they shove him, he hits the pavement hard, the rough ground scraping his skin. They take everything—his wallet, his phone, his sense of safety. 

In the days that follow, Thomas tries to return to normalcy. He goes back to school, but the laughter of his students feels like an echo from another lifetime. Each time he steps into the classroom, he feels a knot tightening in his stomach. He notices how his hands tremble when he tries to write on the whiteboard, how his voice wavers as he speaks. His students, unaware of the turmoil brewing beneath his calm exterior, continue to ask him questions and share their stories, but Thomas feels disconnected. The joy he once derived from teaching is overshadowed by an overwhelming anxiety that grips him each time he steps out of his house.

The nights are the hardest. Thomas lies in bed, staring at the ceiling, replaying the incident over and over in his mind. He can still hear the taunting voices, feel the sharp pain of the fall. He tries to drown out the memories with the hum of the television, but the flickering images only serve to amplify his sense of isolation. He feels haunted, trapped in a cycle of fear and despair. Sleep eludes him, and when he finally drifts off, he is tormented by vivid nightmares, reliving the robbery in excruciating detail.

As the weeks turn into months, Thomas grapples with his new reality. He avoids the route home, opting for lengthy detours that add time to his commute but spare him the panic that rises in his chest at the thought of facing the place where his life changed. His friends notice the shift in his demeanor but struggle to understand what he is going through. They invite him out, try to engage him in conversation, but Thomas finds himself retreating into silence, unable to articulate the darkness that clouds his thoughts.

At school, he becomes increasingly withdrawn. The vibrant interactions that once characterized his teaching style are replaced by a mechanical routine. He finds himself zoning out during lessons, his mind drifting back to that night. It's as if he is living in a fog, unable to fully connect with his students or the world around him. He fears that if he opens up, if he shares his experience, he will burden others with his pain. So, he hides behind a mask of normalcy, all the while feeling like a ghost of his former self.

Despite the heaviness that lingers in his heart, moments of light still pierce through the darkness. He finds solace in the small victories of his students—the child who finally learns to read, the student who conquers their fear of speaking in front of the class. In those moments, he feels a flicker of hope, a reminder of why he became a teacher in the first place. But as soon as the bell rings and the students file out, the weight of his trauma descends once more, and he is left alone with his thoughts, struggling to reconcile the man he was with the man he has become.
